wine.name: Wynns Black Label Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the one grape the label names, grown on the estate's own Coonawarra vineyards.
wine.sites: A selection of the estate's Cabernet from its terra rossa vineyards, red loam over soft limestone on the strip north of Penola; vines planted in the 1950s and 1960s shape the wine.
wine.making: Drawn from a selection of the estate's Cabernet, the wine is matured for twelve to eighteen months, by vintage, in oak. Older vintages used French and American oak; later ones French alone, mostly hogsheads with some barriques and a small share in large vats, a fifth to a third of it new and the rest seasoned.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and mulberry over violet, mint and cedar, at times a black olive note; medium in body, with fine, powdery tannin, fresh acidity and a firm, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps for fifteen years and more in a strong vintage, the fruit giving way to cedar, tobacco and dried mint.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Wynns Coonawarra Estate grew around John Riddoch's triple gabled winery of the 1890s and has made Black Label, Cabernet Sauvignon from its own terra rossa, since 1954. There is blackcurrant, mint and cedar here, medium in body with fine tannin, in a wine that drinks young and keeps fifteen years.
records.story: On Yallum, a large pastoral run near Penola, John Riddoch (1827 to 1901), a Scottish born pastoralist, settled in 1861. In 1890 he subdivided part of it, a strip of red soil over limestone, as the Penola Fruit Colony, blocks for settlers to plant with fruit and vines, and in the 1890s he built the triple gabled winery around which the estate grew. The colony struggled, far from the large markets, and in the decades after his death in 1901 much of his land, the house says, went back to grazing. In 1951 the Wynn family, Melbourne wine merchants, bought the run down winery and its vineyards and renamed the property Wynns Coonawarra Estate. Their Cabernet of the 1954 vintage, the wine later sold as Black Label, began the line, and the gables of Riddoch's winery came to mark its label. In 1982 the house added John Riddoch Cabernet Sauvignon, a separate selection named for the founder. Black Label has been made in most years since: by the house's count the 2018 was its sixty third vintage. In Black Label the strip's way with Cabernet is plain to taste: cool grown, firm and long lived, from red soil over limestone.

wine.name: Katnook Odyssey Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, named alone on the label, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: Specific rows of the estate's own vineyards on Coonawarra's terra rossa, red loam over limestone, on land that was once part of John Riddoch's pastoral holding.
wine.making: Only vintages the house judges strong enough give an Odyssey. For many years the wine spent thirty months and more in barriques, mostly French with some American, part of it new; vintages of the early 2020s spent fifteen to sixteen months in French oak hogsheads, a third or more of them new.
wine.glass: Mulberry, cassis and ripe plum with cedar and a touch of mint; full in body, with supple but defined tannin, fresh acidity and a firm, persistent finish.
wine.ageing: Its first years are tight and firm, and it is made for the cellar: the house's notes give it from ten to twenty years and more, by vintage.
wine.serve: At 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a Bordeaux glass; a young bottle wants an hour or two in a decanter, an old one gentle decanting off its sediment.

records.table: Only in years it judges strong enough does Katnook Estate make Odyssey, from chosen rows of Cabernet Sauvignon on its own terra rossa, aged in French oak. It is built for the cellar, full and firm with cassis, mulberry and cedar, so decant a young bottle.
records.story: Katnook's first wines were made in sheds: by the house's account a small first vintage in 1895 in a nursery shed, and a larger one in 1896 in the Katnook woolshed, with a trained winemaker in charge. The land had been part of the pastoral holding of John Riddoch (1827 to 1901), who had made his home near Penola in 1861 and had a woolshed built there in the 1860s; in 1890 he turned part of it into the Penola Fruit Colony, where vines were planted from 1891. When Riddoch died in 1901, the house relates, the property returned to sheep and the woolshed to wool for decades. New vines were planted in 1971, and in 1980, as the house dates it, the estate made its first commercial vintage of the modern era, again in the woolshed. Odyssey began with the 1991 vintage, held back and released in 1996 to mark a hundred years since the woolshed vintage of 1896; the name, the house says, stands for the estate's journey. Made only in years the house judges strong enough, from chosen rows of its own Cabernet, it stands beside a Shiraz, Prodigy, at the head of the range. Pour it as the wine that joins Riddoch's first Coonawarra vintages to the modern strip.

wine.name: Parker First Growth
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with a small share of Merlot or Petit Verdot in some vintages.
wine.sites: The Abbey Vineyard, planted in 1985 at the southern end of Coonawarra's terra rossa strip, with an old South Australian selection of Cabernet that the house traces to Bordeaux cuttings brought before phylloxera.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the house judges able to age fifteen years and more. Fermented in closed static fermenters, the wine stays on its skins for a month to six weeks in all, by vintage; it is then pressed into French oak, mostly new barriques with some hogsheads, and aged sixteen to eighteen months.
wine.glass: Cigar box, cedar and bay leaf with blackcurrant, mulberry and black olive; full and tightly built, with firm, fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Fifteen years and more is the span the house makes it for, and it is firm and closed when young.
wine.serve: Allow a young bottle two hours in a decanter and decant an old one gently off its sediment; serve at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius in a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Parker Coonawarra Estate named First Growth for Bordeaux's rank: a Cabernet Sauvignon from the Abbey Vineyard at the southern end of the terra rossa, made only in vintages fit to age. Give it time and a decanter: it is firm and fine, with blackcurrant, cedar and bay leaf.
records.story: The Parker family came late to Coonawarra, almost a century after John Riddoch (1827 to 1901) founded the Penola Fruit Colony in 1890. In 1985 the family planted the Abbey Vineyard at the southern end of the terra rossa strip, with Cabernet Sauvignon of an old South Australian selection that the house traces to cuttings brought from Bordeaux before phylloxera. Their aim, the house recalls, was a Coonawarra Cabernet to stand beside Bordeaux, and they named their wine for the Bordeaux rank: in the 1855 classification of the Médoc, the first growths head the list. The first vintage, the 1988, was released under the name Terra Rossa First Growth, and the house has made it only in years it judged fit to age fifteen years and more, mostly Cabernet with a little Merlot or Petit Verdot. Later labels shortened the name to First Growth, and some add Cabernet Sauvignon. The name is a claim, not a rank: Australia has no official classification of growths, and a guest who sees the words on a list is owed that distinction along with the wine, a firm Coonawarra Cabernet from one vineyard, matured in mostly new French barriques.

wine.name: Majella The Malleea
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, a little over half, with Shiraz for the rest.
wine.sites: The Lynn family's Majella vineyard on the terra rossa of the Coonawarra strip, planted from 1968, mostly to Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz.
wine.making: The house makes it only in years it judges right. Small parcels ferment for about five days in headed down static fermenters, then move into new French oak, mostly hogsheads, to finish their fermentation; they mature there for sixteen to twenty two months, by vintage, and chosen barrels make the final blend. Vintages of the early 2000s spent as long as twenty nine months.
wine.glass: Plum, blackcurrant and boysenberry with mocha, cedar and mint; rich and full bodied, with fine, firm tannin and length in the finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy within a few years of release, it is made to keep: the house gives it fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius in a large Bordeaux glass; give a young bottle an hour or two in the decanter.

label.means: The house glosses it as an Aboriginal word for a green paddock, for the pastures of the region.

records.table: Majella's The Malleea joins two grapes from the Lynn family's own terra rossa, Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, finished in new French oak and made only in years that suit it. Rich and firm, with blackcurrant, plum, mocha and mint, it is a wine to decant and keep.
records.story: The Lynns had lived around Penola for generations, by the house's account as storekeepers and then graziers, when one of the family bought the property called Majella from his uncle in 1960. In 1968 his sons planted its first vines on the terra rossa, with their father's blessing, and from the 1970s they sold their grapes to the wineries of the district, Wynns among them. For two decades they were growers only. In 1991 they kept back enough Shiraz to make a wine of their own, made at the Brand family's Laira winery nearby, and the first Majella Shiraz was released. The Malleea followed with the 1996 vintage: Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz from the family's own vineyard, finished in new French oak and made only in years when the growing season suits it. The house glosses the name as an Aboriginal word for a green paddock, for the pastures of the Limestone Coast. The family finished its own winery on the farm at the end of 1998, the house records. A region known for Cabernet shows its Shiraz here too, in a blend that turns a grower family's long knowledge of one vineyard into a label of its own.

wine.name: Lindeman's Limestone Ridge Shiraz Cabernet
wine.grapes: Shiraz, from a little over half to some four fifths by vintage, with Cabernet Sauvignon for the rest; the label names the larger share first.
wine.sites: The Limestone Ridge vineyard in central Coonawarra, planted in the late 1960s on terra rossa over the ridge of limestone that gives it its name.
wine.making: Matured in oak for up to eighteen months, by vintage: for many years in American oak, part of it new and the rest seasoned, and in later vintages in a mix of new and seasoned American and French oak.
wine.glass: Liquorice, blackberry and blackcurrant with a lift of mint and the vanilla of American oak; medium to full in body, with firm, fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Built to age and firm in youth, it trades blackberry for cedar, leather and dried mint over a decade and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The vineyard, named for the ridge of limestone beneath its terra rossa.
The house's name for three Coonawarra reds: Limestone Ridge, St George and Pyrus.

records.table: One of the house's Coonawarra Trio, Lindeman's Limestone Ridge is a Shiraz Cabernet from one vineyard, planted in the late 1960s on terra rossa over a ridge of limestone. In the glass it gives blackcurrant, blackberry and liquorice, firm and long lived, and it is worth decanting.
records.story: Dr Henry John Lindeman (1811 to 1881), an English surgeon trained at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London, sailed as a ship's surgeon before settling in New South Wales on Cawarra, a property on the Paterson River in the Hunter Valley. He planted his first vines there in 1843, the year the house takes as its founding, and after his death at Cawarra in 1881 his sons carried the business on. The house grew far beyond the Hunter, and in the 1950s it began buying Coonawarra wine for blending. In 1965 it bought the Redman family's Rouge Homme winery, its label and its vineyards, and so arrived in Coonawarra, where it went on to add the St George, Limestone Ridge and Nursery vineyards on the terra rossa of the central strip. Limestone Ridge, planted in the late 1960s and named for the ridge of limestone under its red soil, gave a Shiraz Cabernet; St George gave a Cabernet whose 1980 vintage won the Jimmy Watson Trophy for young reds. With Pyrus, a Cabernet blend, they became the three wines the house calls its Coonawarra Trio. Limestone Ridge keeps the old South Australian pairing of Shiraz with Cabernet, from one vineyard with its name on the label.

report: The first vintage of the Limestone Ridge wine was not found in any source read, so the record gives none; the house's history page shows a bottle of the 1979.

One account dates the planting of Limestone Ridge to 1967 and 1968, mostly Shiraz with a little Cabernet, St George to 1969, and explains the name by limestone that made the ground hard to prepare; the Coonawarra Vignerons' pages give no year, so the record says the late 1960s, as Langton's and a merchant listing give it, and leaves the rest out.
The plan's why says the house was founded in 1843; that is the Hunter Valley planting at Cawarra, and the record says so, with the house's arrival in Coonawarra in 1965.

The purchase of Rouge Homme in 1965 rests on the Coonawarra Vignerons' pages and the Redman family's own history; the return of the Rouge Homme brand to the Redman family in May 2026 is left out as recent.

The making is from merchant listings: eighteen months for 2008 and 2009, part new and part seasoned American oak for 2009, and new and seasoned American and French oak later; the refuter cut stainless steel and hogsheads, found in one listing each, and the twelve months of 1988.

A Langton's listing names a 1990 Classic Release as Cabernet Shiraz; the refuter found Shiraz shares of 60 per cent for 1986, 54 for 1994, 83 for 1997 and about four fifths later, so grapes gives the range.

The St George Cabernet Sauvignon 1980 won the Jimmy Watson Trophy by the Coonawarra Vignerons, Wikipedia and Melbourne Royal's list; Wikipedia gives the award to 1981 and Melbourne Royal's list sets it in its 1980 row, so the record gives the vintage and no award year.
